source_text: Καὶ πόσῳ χρησιμώτερον τὸ ἐναντίον, ἱκανὰ κεκτημένον αὐτόν τε περὶ τὴν κτῆσιν μὴ κακοπαθεῖν καὶ οἷς καθῆκεν ἐπικουρεῖν; τίς γὰρ ἂν κοινωνία καταλείποιτο παρὰ ἀνθρώποις, εἰ μηδεὶς ἔχοι μηδέν; πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τοῦτο τὸ δόγμα πολλοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ καλοῖς τοῦ κυρίου δόγμασιν οὐχὶ φανερῶς ἐναντιούμενον εὑρίσκοιτο καὶ μαχόμενον; »ποιήσατε ἑαυτοῖς φίλους ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας, ἵν᾿ ὅταν ἐκλίπῃ, δέξωνται ὑμᾶς εἰς τὰς αἰωνίους σκηνάς.« »κτήσασθε θησαυροὺς ἐν οὐρανῷ, ὅπου μήτε σὴς μήτε βρῶσις ἀφανίζει μήτε κλέπται διορύσσουσι.« πῶς ἄν τις πεινῶντα τρέφοι καὶ διψῶντα ποτίζοι καὶ γυμνὸν σκεπάζοι καὶ ἄστεγον συνάγοι, ἃ τοῖς μὴ ποιήσασιν ἀπειλεῖ πῦρ καὶ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον, εἰ πάντων αὐτὸς ἕκαστος φθάνοι τούτων ὑστερῶν; ἀλλὰ μὴν αὐτός τε ἐπιξενοῦται Ζακχαίῳ καὶ Λευεὶ καὶ Ματθαίῳ τοῖς πλουσίοις καὶ τελώναις, καὶ τὰ μὲν χρήματα αὐτοὺς οὐ κελεύει μεθεῖναι, τὴν δὲ δικαίαν χρῆσιν ἐπιθεὶς καὶ τὴν ἄδικον ἀφελὼν καταγγέλλει· »σήμερον σωτηρία τῷ οἴκῳ τούτῳ.« οὕτω τὴν χρείαν αὐτῶν ἐπαινεῖ, ὥστε καὶ μετὰ τῆς προσθήκης ταύτης τὴν κοινωνίαν ἐπιτάσσει, ποτίζειν τὸν διψῶντα, ἄρτον διδόναι τῷ πεινῶντι, ὑποδέχεσθαι τὸν ἄστεγον, ἀμφιεννύναι τὸν γυμνόν. εἰ δὲ τὰς χρείας οὐχ οἶόν τε ἐκπληροῦν ταύτας μὴ ἀπὸ χρημάτων, τῶν δὲ χρημάτων ἀφίστασθαι κελεύει, τί ἂν ἕτερον εἴη ποιῶν ὁ κύριος ἢ τὰ αὐτὰ διδόναι τε καὶ μὴ διδόναι παραινῶν, τρέφειν καὶ μὴ τρέφειν, ὑποδέχεσθαι καὶ ἀποκλείειν, κοινωνεῖν καὶ μὴ κοινωνεῖν, ὅπερ ἁπάντων ἀλογώτατον.
thought_title: Wealth as a means of mutual aid
orientation: Clement is arguing that the command to sell one's possessions cannot mean literal poverty, because such poverty would make the commanded acts of charity impossible.
pass_a_gloss: And how much more useful is the opposite, having sufficient possessions, both for oneself not to suffer hardship over the possession and to help those to whom it is fitting? For what sharing would be left among human beings, if no one had anything? And how would this teaching not be found clearly opposing and fighting against many other good teachings of the Lord? "Make for yourselves friends from the worldly wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal tents." "Acquire treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys nor thieves break in." How could anyone feed the hungry and give drink to the thirsty and clothe the naked and take in the homeless, things for which he threatens fire and outer darkness to those who have not done them, if each person himself were first lacking all these things? But indeed he himself is received as a guest by Zacchaeus and Levi and Matthew, rich persons and tax collectors, and he does not command them to let go of their money, but imposing the just use and taking away the unjust use he proclaims: "Today salvation has come to this house." Thus he praises the use of their resources, so that also with this addition he commands the sharing, to give drink to the thirsty, to give bread to the hungry, to receive the homeless, to clothe the naked. But if it is not possible to fulfill these needs without money, and he commands to stand away from money, what else would the Lord be doing than advising to give and not to give the same things, to feed and not to feed, to receive and to shut out, to share and not to share, which is the most irrational of all things.

choices.why: The glossary requires this rendering for the term, avoiding 'unrighteous mammon' or 'dishonest wealth'.
The glossary requires 'money' for χρήματα, distinguishing it from possessions (κτήματα).
The glossary requires 'rich person' for πλούσιος, and the plural here refers to Zacchaeus, Levi, and Matthew.
The glossary requires 'salvation' for σωτηρία, and it is used in the quoted words of Jesus.
Renders the superlative force of the adjective, emphasizing the absurdity of the contradictory commands.

pass_b_english: And how much more useful is the opposite: to have enough, so that you neither suffer hardship over your possessions yourself nor fail to help those you ought to help? For what sharing would be left among human beings if no one had anything? How could this teaching not be found plainly opposed to many other fine teachings of the Lord, and fighting against them? "Make friends for yourselves by means of worldly wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings" (Luke 16:9). "Store up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal" (Matthew 6:20). How could anyone feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, or take in the homeless—things for which he threatens fire and outer darkness to those who do not do them—if each person were already lacking all these things himself? But the Lord himself is received as a guest by Zacchaeus and Levi and Matthew, rich persons and tax collectors, and he does not command them to let go of their money. Instead, he imposes the just use of it and takes away the unjust use, and he declares, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). He praises their use of money so much that he commands sharing with this addition: give drink to the thirsty, give bread to the hungry, take in the homeless, clothe the naked. But if it is not possible to fulfill these needs without money, and he commands us to give up money, what else would the Lord be doing but urging the same things to be given and not given, to feed and not to feed, to take in and to shut out, to share and not to share—which is the most irrational thing of all.
